units.title: Leader-follower, multi-leader and leaderless replication
outcomes: Trace a write and its acknowledgement through each of the three replication topologies.
Choose write authority, read routing and conflict handling for a disconnected client.
Explain why a coordinator in a leaderless store is not an ordering leader.
units.why: Build on Replication, quorums and consensus vocabulary. The new job is to turn each topology into an operation path and identify exactly where writes can diverge.

next.note: Specify what each acknowledgement on the path means.

study.title: DDIA, 2nd edition: the three replication architectures
study.locator: Chapter 6, Replication: Single-Leader Replication, pp. 198 to 200; Multi-Leader Replication through Sync Engines and Local-First Software, pp. 215 to 222; Leaderless Replication, pp. 229 to 230
study.depth: Review the single-leader path from Systems briefly. Read the multi-leader topology and local-first discussion closely; stop before Dealing with Conflicting Writes.

focus: Separate write authority from network shape. Several shard leaders are not several leaders for the same key.
An asynchronously connected multi-leader store can acknowledge conflicting writes independently. It needs both dissemination and a conflict policy.
A leaderless coordinator gathers replica responses. That role alone does not impose a common write order.
Loop suppression and dependency ordering are different jobs. Deduplicating a forwarded update does not ensure that its prerequisite has arrived.
units.reproduce: Draw three local replicas and two clients, with a partition separating one replica from the others. For each topology, trace two writes to the same key and a subsequent read on each side. Mark who may acknowledge, which replicas hold each version, and which read outcomes depend on an as-yet-unspecified conflict or quorum rule. Do not give a topology a consistency label until those rules are stated.
traps: Calling all-to-all forwarding leaderless when each node independently orders and accepts local writes as a leader.
Assuming an extra replica improves write availability when the acknowledgement rule still waits for every replica.
Treating a topology diagram as a durability or freshness contract.

selfTest.q: Does a client contacting only one coordinator imply single-leader replication?
selfTest.a: No. The coordinator may fan out to interchangeable replicas without assigning a common order. Write authority and ordering, not the client connection count, distinguish the designs.

selfTest.q: Can a disconnected multi-leader replica accept edits without proving that they preserve a global uniqueness constraint?
selfTest.a: Yes, but accepting edits independently does not enforce unrestricted global uniqueness. The design needs coordination, preallocated disjoint authority, or an explicit conflict outcome.

selfTest.q: Why can an insert and a dependent update arrive in the wrong order in an all-to-all topology?
selfTest.a: They can travel over different links with different delays. Redundant paths do not themselves carry or enforce the dependency.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: configurable write authority and read routing in the local loglab replicated-store model, with topology-specific partition histories.
units.stopWhen: Your three path diagrams identify every acknowledgement and divergent version, and you can state which missing policy prevents predicting a read result.

fit.note: DDIA supplies the topology and dependency cases beyond the Systems introduction; the mini-project turns the paths into executable policies.

units.title: Synchronous and asynchronous acknowledgement, replication logs, positions and lag
outcomes: Specify receipt, persistence and application as separate acknowledgement boundaries.
Compare statement, physical and logical replication logs for deterministic replay and version coupling.
Measure position lag without misreporting it as elapsed-time staleness.
units.why: The local durability boundary from Storage engines and recovery is only one step in a replicated write. Separate received, persisted and applied positions before claiming what survives a crash or what a follower read can see.

next.note: Use the acknowledged boundary to decide whether promotion loses a write.

study.title: DDIA, 2nd edition: acknowledgement and log representation
study.locator: Chapter 6, Replication: Synchronous Versus Asynchronous Replication, pp. 200 to 201; Implementation of Replication Logs, pp. 206 to 208; Monitoring staleness, pp. 234 to 235

focus: Synchronous says the leader waits for a specified replica event, not that every copy is durable or queryable. Name that event and the replicas required.
Statement replay needs deterministic inputs and ordering. A physical log couples replicas to storage format; a logical log describes changes at a less storage-specific boundary.
Compare positions only within the same log lineage and in the same units. Byte positions, record counts and time lag are different metrics.
A follower can have received or persisted a suffix that it has not applied. Read routing must use the boundary relevant to visibility.
units.reproduce: In Python 3, model a single ordered log with six records and no failover. Give a follower received, persisted and applied positions of 6, 4 and 2. Assert that its durable backlog relative to the leader's durable position 6 is two records, while its unapplied backlog is four. Crash the follower by clearing volatile state, recover through position 4, then replay the suffix. Keep separate counters rather than a single lag value. These are record positions, not seconds.
traps: Inferring read visibility from a persistence acknowledgement without waiting for application.
Subtracting positions across diverged leader histories after failover.
Reporting zero position lag as zero wall-clock read latency or as proof that no writes were lost.

selfTest.q: A follower confirms receipt in memory. Does that confirm survival of its process crash?
selfTest.a: No. The contract must require stable storage if the acknowledgement is meant to survive that crash. Receipt alone is insufficient.

selfTest.q: Can two replicas execute the same timestamp-producing statement and diverge?
selfTest.a: Yes, if each evaluates a nondeterministic time function independently. Replicate its chosen result or otherwise make execution deterministic.

selfTest.q: Why can a follower be 100 records behind without a known time lag?
selfTest.a: Record positions do not encode elapsed time. You need write timing and an explicit visibility boundary; the workload may be bursty or idle.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: separate receive, persist, apply and acknowledgement events, with record-lag measurements and a crash between receipt and persistence.
units.stopWhen: Your trace distinguishes the two-record durable backlog from the four-record unapplied backlog and shows which acknowledgement modes survive the injected crash.

fit.note: DDIA covers acknowledgement choices, three log formats and position monitoring; the mini-project supplies boundary-specific instrumentation and crash practice.

units.title: Failover, stale-leader risk and replica rejoin and replacement
outcomes: Construct a failover history that loses an asynchronously acknowledged write.
Implement a snapshot-position and suffix catch-up path for a replacement replica.
Reject stale authority and distinguish a returning replica from an empty replacement.
units.why: Build on the fencing and incarnation results from Time, identity, membership and failure. Here the test is whether those boundaries survive promotion, divergent logs and replica replacement, not whether a timeout elects a leader.

next.note: Carry the stale-authority case into a consensus-backed design.

study.title: DDIA, 2nd edition: bootstrap, catch-up and promotion
study.locator: Chapter 6, Replication: Setting Up New Followers, pp. 201 to 202; Handling Node Outages, pp. 204 to 206; Chapter 10, Consistency and Consensus: Implementing Linearizable Systems, pp. 411 to 413
study.depth: Skip the object-storage architecture sidebar on pp. 202 to 203. Read the Chapter 10 passage for stale-leader and lost-write boundaries, not a consensus implementation.

focus: A snapshot needs an exact position in a particular log lineage. Copying files while writes continue is not a consistent bootstrap procedure.
A replica missing retained history needs a new snapshot. A replacement must not inherit the old process's acknowledgements merely by reusing its address.
A timeout supplies suspicion, not exclusive authority. In this model, an explicit controller changes the epoch and the mutation boundary enforces it; distributed election comes later.
A rejoining old leader may carry an acknowledged but unreplicated suffix. Preserve that evidence before discarding, reconciling or rejecting it according to the contract.
units.reproduce: Using Python 3 and an explicit controller, acknowledge a write on the old leader while replication is blocked. Promote a follower that lacks it, then read the old value. Record the resulting linearizability violation. Rejoin the old leader with its divergent suffix: block its writes using the current epoch, preserve the discarded suffix in the evidence, and rebuild it from a consistent snapshot plus the new leader's suffix. Repeat bootstrap with an empty replacement and with a gap in retained history; require a fresh snapshot for the gap.
traps: Treating the largest numeric offset as freshest when two leaders have different log lineages.
Generating a higher epoch locally without an authority that prevents competing promotions.
Letting an empty replacement count toward a quorum before transferring the data that earlier acknowledgements depended on.

selfTest.q: Does fencing the old leader recover its lost acknowledged write?
selfTest.a: No. Fencing prevents future stale-authority effects. It cannot supply data that the promoted follower never received.

selfTest.q: Why must a snapshot carry its replication-log position?
selfTest.a: The new replica needs to know exactly where replay begins. Otherwise it may omit updates or apply updates already reflected in the snapshot.

selfTest.q: A follower requests a suffix that has been deleted. Can it safely skip to the current end?
selfTest.a: No. That would omit state changes. Transfer a consistent snapshot and then replay the retained suffix belonging to it.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: controller-driven promotion, stale-epoch rejection, divergent-leader rejoin and empty-replica snapshot bootstrap in loglab.
units.stopWhen: Your tests expose the lost-write history, reject the stale leader, and rebuild both a returning replica and an empty replacement without skipping a log gap.

fit.note: DDIA locates snapshot bootstrap, retention gaps and failover hazards; the mini-project implements them under an explicit controller rather than prematurely claiming consensus.

units.title: Stale reads, read-your-writes and monotonic read and write guarantees
outcomes: Separate read-your-writes, monotonic reads, monotonic writes and writes-follow-reads using histories.
Implement a session frontier that routes or waits for a sufficiently advanced replica.
Diagnose a session violation after rerouting or losing client context.
units.why: Consistency models and conflict resolution introduced session guarantees. This unit implements the eligibility test, including what happens when no reachable replica contains the session's dependencies.

next.note: Extend session-local dependencies to causal visibility across clients.

study.title: DDIA, 2nd edition: replica routing for sessions
study.locator: Chapter 6, Replication: Problems with Replication Lag through Solutions for Replication Lag, pp. 209 to 215
study.depth: Use the familiar stale-read examples as routing tests, not a second introduction. Stop before Multi-Leader Replication.

study.title: Terry et al. (1994): session contracts and enforcement
study.locator: Sections 3.1 to 3.4, the four guarantees; Section 4, Providing the guarantees; Section 5, Practical implementation of the guarantees, including Figure 1

focus: Read-your-writes requires a read view that includes the session's prior writes, not necessarily their unchanged values after other writes supersede them.
Monotonic reads tracks previously observed history. Monotonic writes orders the session's writes at replicas; writes-follow-reads carries dependencies from reads into later writes.
Use an applied log position for a single ordered lineage or a dependency vector for multiple origins. A frontier must describe a complete prefix, not merely the largest event observed.
The paper's enforcement relies on ordered propagation and session metadata. If no eligible replica is reachable, preserve the guarantee by waiting or failing rather than silently using a stale one.
units.reproduce: In a Python 3 model of one log lineage, implement a session token storing the greatest required applied position. After the session writes at position 4, offer replicas applied through positions 2 and 5: only the second is eligible for a read-your-writes read. After reading through position 5, reject the first replica for monotonic reads even if the session made no new write. For monotonic writes, delay a second write at a new replica until its first write is included. Preserve the token across rerouting, then erase it deliberately and retain the violating trace.
traps: Using sticky routing as a complete guarantee when the chosen replica can restart, roll back or be replaced.
Comparing returned numeric values to test monotonic reads. A later legitimate write may lower the value.
Confusing the order in which the client sends writes with the order in which every replica exposes them.

selfTest.q: Can a session satisfy monotonic reads while always reading stale data?
selfTest.a: Yes. Its observed histories must not move backward, but they need not be globally current.

selfTest.q: Does read-your-writes alone require a replica serving a later write to include all earlier reads?
selfTest.a: No. Writes-follow-reads carries those read dependencies into the write. Read-your-writes constrains subsequent reads relative to the session's writes.

selfTest.q: Why can satisfying a session guarantee reduce availability after a partition?
selfTest.a: The reachable replicas may lack the required history. Serving them immediately would violate the guarantee, so the operation must wait, fail, or reach an eligible replica.

selfTest.q: Does a write on a phone automatically enter the browser's session token?
selfTest.a: No. Cross-device guarantees need a shared or transferred session context. A common user name alone does not transfer dependencies.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: session-frontier routing, waiting on lagging replicas and tests for context loss during rerouting in loglab.
units.stopWhen: Your session tests reject an ineligible replica after both a write and a read, and distinguish monotonic-write ordering from read-your-writes visibility.

fit.note: DDIA supplies routing cases and Terry supplies all four definitions plus vector-based enforcement; loglab provides the implementation and negative histories.

units.title: Linearizability as a history property and sequential consistency
outcomes: Derive a legal sequential witness or an ordering contradiction for a register history.
Distinguish process-order constraints from real-time precedence.
Explain per-object composition and the treatment of incomplete operations.
units.why: The earlier Systems card classified simple stale reads. Now derive the history definition that a checker must implement, including why all reads must fit one order rather than each choosing a convenient replica view.

next.note: Implement witness search against the formal history definition.

study.title: Herlihy and Wing (1990): definition and locality
study.locator: Sections 1 through 3.1, printed pp. 463 to 471; concentrate on 2.1 Histories, 2.2 Definition of Linearizability and Theorem 1 in 3.1 Locality
study.depth: Stop before Section 3.2. Translate the queue examples into ordering constraints; do not implement a concurrent queue.

study.title: Jepsen: sequential consistency
study.locator: Sequential Consistency and Formally (page read 2026-10-15)

study.title: MIT 6.5840 Spring 2026, Lecture 8: Consistency, Linearizability
study.locator: definition: a history through example 6, including the serial register specification
study.depth: Answer each history question before reading its discussion. In example 3, the sentence saying no assignment works for example 2 is a numbering typo: example 2 permits the old read; example 3 is the contradictory history.

focus: Both models need a legal total order that preserves each process's program order. Linearizability also preserves every response-before-invocation edge across processes.
An incomplete operation can be completed in an extension or omitted when forming the complete history. Never require its effect to be absent just because its client timed out.
Locality lets linearizable object histories compose. It does not turn separate calls into an atomic multi-object transaction.
Build on Threads, interleavings and memory consistency for program order, but do not equate distributed register semantics with a language's relaxed memory model.
units.reproduce: Start a register at 0, with exactly one write of 1 and one write of 2 by separate clients. Both writes remain pending while reader P reads 1 then 2, and reader Q reads 2 then 1; all four reads complete before either write returns. Derive why no sequentially consistent order exists: P forces the write of 1 before the write of 2, while Q forces the reverse. Then remove Q's reads and give a legal linearization of the remaining history. Separately, consider just a completed write of 1 followed in real time by another client's read of 0, initially 0: explain why sequential consistency can permit that history while linearizability cannot.
traps: Checking each read independently. A collection of individually plausible reads can have no common legal order.
Sorting calls by invocation time or server log time and treating that one order as the definition.
Claiming that a clean finite history proves the implementation linearizable for all executions.

selfTest.q: Can sequential consistency put a read before another client's already completed write?
selfTest.a: Yes, if it preserves each process's program order and the register specification. Linearizability additionally enforces the cross-process real-time edge.

selfTest.q: Why does removing Q make the pending-writes example legal?
selfTest.a: The order write 1, P's read of 1, write 2, P's read of 2 fits all intervals and the object specification. Q supplied the contradictory order.

selfTest.q: Is an operation's actual internal execution instant needed to check linearizability?
selfTest.a: No. The observed history needs some legal order with points inside invocation-response intervals. The witness need not identify the implementation's actual instant.

selfTest.q: What does the locality theorem not provide for two separately linearizable account registers?
selfTest.a: It does not make a debit and credit across them one atomic transfer. That requires a specification and mechanism for the combined operation or transaction.

practice.name: Cambridge Concurrent and Distributed Systems: Exercise 20
practice.locator: Michaelmas 2021/22, Section 7.2: Exercise 20 on p. 74 and its execution diagram on p. 75
practice.note: First draw real-time and value-order edges. Give a witness or contradiction before consulting the Section 7.2 discussion. This is a paper exercise, not an autograded test.

units.stopWhen: You solve Exercise 20 with explicit ordering constraints and can separate a sequential-consistency witness from a linearizability witness without relying on server internals.

fit.note: Herlihy-Wing gives the definition and composition theorem, Jepsen distinguishes sequential consistency, and the verified Cambridge exercise supplies history practice.

units.title: Causal and eventual consistency, convergence and CRDT vocabulary
outcomes: Reject a causal-visibility violation even when all replicas eventually converge.
State the propagation and conflict-resolution assumptions behind eventual convergence.
Distinguish state-based merge from operation-based delivery and their convergence requirements.
units.why: Convergence answers whether copies agree after propagation, not whether intermediate observations preserve dependencies. Use a concrete causal+ design to separate those two obligations.

next.note: Implement and validate a CRDT after learning its delivery and merge assumptions.

study.title: DDIA, 2nd edition: convergence versus dependency order
study.locator: Chapter 6, Replication: Consistent prefix reads, pp. 213 to 214; Automatic conflict resolution through Conflict-free replicated datatypes and operational transformation, pp. 226 to 228

study.title: Lloyd et al., COPS (SOSP 2011): causal+ and dependency checks
study.locator: Section 3.1 Definition, Section 3.3 Causal+ in COPS, Sections 4.1 to 4.3, including Figure 6
study.depth: Stop before COPS-GT. Track dependency metadata and remote visibility; do not build a multi-datacenter deployment.

study.title: Preguica, Baquero and Shapiro (2018): CRDT synchronization vocabulary
study.locator: Synchronization Model, printed pp. 6 to 7, covering state-based and operation-based replication
study.depth: Vocabulary only. Defer a full CRDT implementation and proofs to the linked later unit.

focus: A receiver may need to hold a dependent version until its prerequisites are visible. Delivery order and visibility order need not be identical.
Causal+ means causal consistency plus convergent conflict handling. COPS's datacenter-local linearizability is an architectural choice, not the definition of causal+.
State-based CRDTs use inflationary updates and a join on a semilattice; associative, commutative and idempotent merge tolerates reordering and duplicates when state eventually propagates.
Operation-based CRDTs need reliable effect dissemination and the stated ordering assumptions. Commuting concurrent effectors does not make repeated application of a non-idempotent effect harmless.
units.reproduce: Draw a post write, another client's read of that post, and that client's reply write. Deliver the reply before the post to a third replica. Show that immediate reply visibility violates causality even if later propagation makes all replicas agree; then add a dependency check that delays visibility. Separately, merge grow-only counter states \((2,0)\) and \((0,3)\) by componentwise maximum: both orders and a duplicate merge give \((2,3)\), whose query is 5. Explain why adding the two whole states repeatedly would double-count.
traps: Calling eventual convergence a bound on staleness or a guarantee during a permanent partition.
Assuming every CRDT provides causal reads across independently replicated objects.
Calling reliable delivery sufficient for an increment effector when duplicates may be applied twice.

selfTest.q: Can two independent concurrent writes appear in different orders under causal consistency?
selfTest.a: Yes. Causality alone does not order independent writes. A separate convergence policy determines how conflicting versions are reconciled.

selfTest.q: Why is componentwise maximum idempotent but repeated addition is not?
selfTest.a: Taking the maximum with the same component again changes nothing. Adding it again counts that contribution again.

selfTest.q: Does an operation-based CRDT always require causal delivery?
selfTest.a: No. Requirements depend on its effectors. Causal delivery plus commuting concurrent effectors is a common sufficient condition; without ordering, all reordered effectors must commute. Duplicate application needs a separate argument.

selfTest.q: What extra property does causal+ name beyond causal consistency?
selfTest.a: Convergence through consistent conflict handling. It does not mean linearizability or bounded replication lag.

practice.name: Gossip Glomers Challenge 4: Grow-Only Counter
practice.locator: Specification, Service: seq-kv and Evaluation; three local nodes with the g-counter workload and partition nemesis
practice.note: Use Go and Maelstrom v0.2.4 on your machine; record the actual installed version. The page was tested on 0.2.3. Start from its stateless counter contract over sequentially consistent storage, not an assumed in-memory CRDT requirement. The checker checks successful final reads against confirmed and possible indeterminate increments; it does not establish intermediate-read linearizability. Keep the run history and add your own dependency-visibility test in loglab.

units.stopWhen: Challenge 4 passes its final-count check, you explain its weaker intermediate-read contract, and your post/reply trace distinguishes eventual agreement from causal visibility.

fit.note: COPS provides an enforceable causal+ mechanism, the overview supplies bounded CRDT vocabulary, and Challenge 4 supplies checked convergence practice without duplicating the later CRDT implementation.

units.title: Availability under partition, quorum intersection and its membership assumptions
outcomes: Derive the fixed-membership intersection bound and identify where its data-retention premise fails.
Construct a new-then-old read history despite intersecting quorums.
Derive the partition availability contradiction for a linearizable register.
units.why: Replication, quorums and consensus vocabulary already derived set overlap. The new work is to show why overlap is not a register protocol, then derive the extra read-back and version rules using ABD.

next.note: Break the fixed-replica assumption deliberately and account for the weaker contract.

study.title: DDIA, 2nd edition: quorum limitations and the read inversion
study.locator: Chapter 6, Replication: Using quorums for reading and writing and Understanding the limitations of quorum consistency, pp. 231 to 234; Chapter 10, Consistency and Consensus: Implementing Linearizable Systems through The Unhelpful CAP Theorem, pp. 411 to 416, especially Figure 10-6
study.depth: Stop before Linearizability and network delays. Do not use the incident percentages as workload assumptions.

study.title: Gilbert and Lynch (2002): the asynchronous impossibility argument
study.locator: Sections 2.1 to 2.3; Section 3.1, Theorem 1 and Corollary 1.1; Section 4, Partially Synchronous Networks
study.depth: Follow the partition execution proof. In Section 4 compare the changed timing assumptions, not every relaxed-consistency construction.

study.title: Cambridge notes: ABD as a quorum protocol
study.locator: Michaelmas 2021/22, Section 7.2, pp. 69 to 73, through Exercise 19
study.depth: Use the single-writer register algorithm as the derivation boundary. Do not generalize it to compare-and-set or transactions.

focus: For one replica universe of size \(N\), read and write response sets satisfy \(|Q_r \cap Q_w| \ge R + W - N\). Overlap needs the same membership and retained acknowledged versions.
A read may reveal a partially propagated write before any write quorum completes. A later read can miss it unless the read protocol stabilizes the version before returning.
ABD uses ordered versions and a quorum write-back during reads. Set intersection is one part of that argument, not a replacement for it.

CAP availability requires every request received by a non-failing node eventually to receive the specified operation response, in every fair execution including lossy ones. Errors or timeouts do not satisfy a successful register operation contract.
units.reproduce: With three fixed replicas initially 0, start a write of 1 that reaches only replica A and remains pending. A read of A and B returns 1; after it completes, a read of B and C returns 0. Derive the linearizability contradiction even though the configured write threshold is three and read threshold is two. Add a synchronous quorum write-back of the greatest ordered version before returning the first read, and show why every later size-two read intersects it. Then reproduce the CAP contradiction: complete a write on one side of a permanent partition and invoke a read on the isolated side, whose observations are indistinguishable from an execution with no write.
traps: Using quorum arithmetic across old and new memberships without a transition protocol or state transfer.
Treating a process that restarted without its acknowledged data as the same durable quorum participant.
Using an observed success fraction as the theorem's universal availability definition.

selfTest.q: For five fixed replicas with three read and three write responses, what does intersection prove?
selfTest.a: The response sets share at least one member. It does not alone prove correct version selection, stability across failures, or linearizability.

selfTest.q: Why does the pending-write inversion violate linearizability even though the write never completed?
selfTest.a: The first read of 1 forces that write before it in any legal completion. Real time places the second read later, so returning 0 without another write is impossible.

selfTest.q: Does an arbitrarily long but finite delay alone force a safety violation?
selfTest.a: No. A linearizable system may wait. The impossibility combines the safety requirement with availability in all permitted executions, including a partition that prevents the needed communication indefinitely.

selfTest.q: What does synchronous read write-back add to mere read quorum overlap?
selfTest.a: It places the observed greatest version on a quorum before exposing it, preventing a later intersecting read from missing that version under the algorithm's version and retention rules.

practice.name: Cambridge Concurrent and Distributed Systems: Exercise 19
practice.locator: Michaelmas 2021/22, Section 7.2, Exercise 19 on p. 73: give pseudocode for ABD
practice.note: Derive the single-writer algorithm from the stated register contract. Annotate where it waits for quorums and why the read's second phase is necessary. The section mini-project tests the no-write-back counterexample against your checker; the exercise has no public autograder.

units.stopWhen: Your ABD pseudocode explains each quorum phase, and you can derive both the pending-write inversion and the partition contradiction without claiming that overlap alone proves linearizability.

fit.note: DDIA supplies the counterexample, Gilbert-Lynch supplies the model and proof, and Cambridge Exercise 19 supplies protocol derivation beyond the prior Systems arithmetic.
